conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in. My name is Maya Carter, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen after a baby is born, and I’m here to make sure you feel heard and supported.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that sometimes show up in the first months postpartum. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between you and our care team unless you tell us something that makes us worry about your safety. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

First question: Over the last seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things the way you normally would, or have you found yourself feeling disappointed or unable to enjoy activities you used to like?

[wrapping the baby-blanket a little tighter around my shoulders]  
Honestly? I can’t remember the last time I got excited about anything. I used to love Sunday brunch with my girlfriends—now just thinking about getting dressed feels like climbing a mountain. Even little things, like watching a show I used to binge, feels… flat, like the color’s been drained out. I’ll try to scroll on my phone or take a walk, but it’s like I’m watching someone else do it. I still go through the motions, but there’s no spark. I keep telling myself it’s just exhaustion, but seven days straight of “meh” is starting to scare me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I *want* to laugh—my husband will make a joke or send me a meme he swears is hilarious—but it feels forced. I’ll smile for a second, then it just drops off. Mostly I feel like I’m faking it so he won’t worry. The last time I actually chuckled was… I don’t even remember.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet shrug, eyes on the baby in the carrier]

No… not really. When I wake up, the first thing I feel is dread about getting through the day. I used to plan little things—coffee runs, a bath, maybe ordering my favorite lunch—but now even those sound exhausting. I tell myself, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel excited again,” but tomorrow keeps feeling the same.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. Yesterday she wouldn’t latch for, like, twenty minutes, and I kept thinking, “I’m already failing at the one thing she needs me to do.” I cried in the glider and told my husband it must be something wrong with me. Even when the dog knocked over the diaper-caddy, I muttered, “Great job, can’t even keep the house safe.” I know rationally it’s not all my fault, but my brain keeps whispering that I’m just not good enough at this mom thing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all day, every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing—so I poke her foot just to watch her stir. Last night I Googled SIDS stats for an hour even though she was right beside me in the bassinet. I know it’s “no good reason,” but in the moment it feels life-or-death, and I can’t turn the fear off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… sometimes it hits out of nowhere. Like, I’ll be folding her onesies and suddenly my chest feels tight, like I can’t get enough air. It’s not about anything specific—just this wave of “something awful is about to happen.” My hands shake and I have to sit down until it passes. It’s scary enough that I avoid going to the store alone because I’m terrified it’ll happen in the checkout line and I’ll be stuck.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Even small chores feel huge—like the bottles piling up in the sink make me want to crawl back into bed. I’ll start one thing, remember three others, and then just stand in the middle of the room frozen. I keep thinking, “How does everyone else manage?” and then the guilt piles on because I’m home all day and still can’t keep up. It’s like I’m drowning in to-do lists I can’t finish.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t stop replaying everything I think I did wrong that day—did I burp her long enough, did I snap at my husband, why didn’t I fold the laundry. Some nights I finally drift off, then her tiny grunt wakes me and I can’t get back to sleep even after she’s settled. I end up staring at the ceiling feeling this heavy sadness, checking the clock every hour. I probably get four broken hours, if that.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be rocking her and tears just start leaking—no real trigger, just this steady ache. I keep thinking I should be soaking up these newborn moments, but instead I feel hollow and guilty for not being happier. I try to perk up when people visit, but as soon as I’m alone, the sadness settles right back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed, but other times it just sneaks up—like I’ll see a diaper commercial and burst into tears. Last night I couldn’t get her to settle and I just sat on the nursery floor sobbing with her in my arms. I try to keep quiet so my husband won’t hear, but it’s getting harder to hide.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes still on the baby]

No—never. I feel low, but I’d never do anything to leave her without a mom. I just want to feel better, not disappear.

You've shared how the joy you once felt-brunches, favorite shows, even simple coffee runs-has been replaced by a heavy gray cloud since your baby arrived. Daily tasks feel like mountains, laughter feels forced, and moments that "should" be special are instead filled with dread, guilt, and tears. Despite your deep love for your daughter, you're exhausted by constant worry, sudden panic, and a sadness that leaks out many times a week, often without warning.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to genuinely laugh, feeling forced smiles and no memory of last chuckle, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory joy and daily dread, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself repeatedly and intensely ('a lot,' 'I'm already failing,' 'can't even keep the house safe'), indicating self-reproach 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, shaking, shortness of breath) that interfere with daily activities, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being overwhelmed "most of the time" and unable to cope with even small tasks, matching the highest-severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly, prolonged difficulty falling and staying asleep driven by persistent unhappiness and rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily pervasive sadness, tearfulness without triggers, and persistent hollow ache—clearly aligns with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a few times a week" and gives vivid examples (commercials, nursery episode), matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 26 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating high likelihood of <med>major depressive episode with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms nearly every day: pervasive anhedonia (<quote>the color's been drained out</quote>), persistent low mood (<quote>steady ache</quote>), excessive self-blame (<quote>I'm already failing</quote>), daily anxiety and panic symptoms, and sleep disruption driven by rumination. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for major depression, and the postpartum timing necessitates urgent assessment. You denied self-harm ideas, so acute safety risk is lower, but functional impairment is significant. <med>EPDS</med> is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> this week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, short-term <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding, and practical support services
3. Arrange reliable daytime help with feeds, meals, and household tasks so you can secure at least one 4-hour block of uninterrupted sleep
4. Practice 5-minute <med>paced breathing</med> or <med>progressive muscle relaxation</med> when panic sensations start; keep a written script nearby
5. Limit doom-scrolling; set a 15-minute evening timer for phone use and switch to calming music or a dim light to protect fragile sleep
6. Share your EPDS results openly with your partner or a trusted family member so they understand this isn't "just exhaustion" and can help coordinate care
7. Book a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress; if thoughts of self-harm develop, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen (EPDS conversation)

Presenting symptoms/concerns endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood with daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)
- Excessive/unwarranted guilt/self-blame (Q3)
- Generalized anxiety, panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Overwhelmed, "frozen," unable to complete routine tasks (Q6)
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)

Associated patterns:
- Guilt/self-criticism pervasive across parenting, household and self-care tasks
- Fearful hypervigilance regarding infant safety
- Functional impairment: avoidance of outings, incomplete chores, broken sleep

Safety:
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10); no current safety concern identified

Screening significance:
Findings consistent with elevated risk for Major Depressive Episode with anxious features in the postpartum period. Recommend use of validated EPDS score for quantification and formal diagnostic assessment by appropriate provider to determine need for treatment/intervention.
